arguments.premise_synthesis: Current US debt-to-GDP is above 120%, similar to post-WWII levels. However, post-WWII debt was reduced to around 30% through various means. If the Federal Reserve were to raise interest rates significantly, interest on the national debt would escalate to $2-3 trillion or more. The US government is currently unable to make even minimum payments and must borrow additional funds, indicating severe fiscal constraints. This high debt burden limits the Fed's ability to use aggressive rate hikes to combat inflation, unlike the Volcker era, making alternative solutions like bank deregulation essential to foster production and reduce inflation.
arguments.conclusion_supported: It is established that high debt-to-GDP restricts monetary policy options, supporting the claim that bank deregulation (removing SLR) is the most effective solution to prevent crisis, reduce stagflation risk, and stimulate economic growth.

arguments.premise_synthesis: Debt-to-GDP exceeded 120% at the peak of WWII, similar to today. However, post-war government spending dropped from 40% of GDP to under 10%, allowing debt reduction through rapid economic growth. In contrast, current government spending is 22-23% of GDP and entitlements like Medicare, Medicaid, and Social Security are increasing, not decreasing. During WWII, production was diverted to destruction, and after the war it shifted to goods people wanted, boosting real wealth. This dynamic does not apply today as spending is not temporary but persistent.
arguments.conclusion_supported: It is established that the post-WWII debt reduction path is not replicable under current fiscal conditions, supporting the claim that bank deregulation (removing SLR) is the most effective solution to prevent a crisis and stimulate economic growth.
